cultural.vision_reason: This is a strip-woven indigo cotton tobe/boubou gown with embroidered chest panel, a garment type worn across West Africa including by the Wolof of Senegal; strip-weaving and indigo boubou robes are common regional dress, so it plausibly belongs to the claimed group even though the museum notes Hausa/Yoruba pattern names.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary: Gown (tobe, boubou, riga), with oblong shaped body with broad sleeves flared towards the top. Composed of 77 narrow strips, which have in the warp a uniform pattern from dark alternating with lighter indigo-dyed handspun thread; the weft is also of indigo. The same strips are used in both warp and weft, although a few of the strips have a different pattern with white instead of light blue and white lines in the weft to create a checked appearance known as ‘saki’ by the Hausa’ and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba. A pocket has been sewn to the front, and both front and back have been embroidered in a white silk thread. The embroidery is in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern, using chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The gown is hemmed around the neck and sleeves. The entire body of the garment is lined with machine-woven blue cotton and the hem is lined with 23 narrow strips which are plain woven using light and dark blue warps and light blue and red alaari wefts.
